brief.topic: The Square Hidden in a Returning Ball

s01: A falling ball returns, but not to where it began.
Ignore air resistance and imagine a rigid, still floor.
Suppose the upward speed after impact is half the downward speed before it.
That does not give half the original height.
Speed gained in falling grows with the square root of height.
Going back upward reverses that relationship.
Half the speed gives one quarter of the height.
This speed ratio is called the coefficient of restitution.
In this simple model, the height ratio is its square.
Energy also changes form during the collision, through deformation, warmth, and sound.
Try a speed ratio of three quarters instead.
The returned height becomes nine sixteenths, a little over half.
Real bounce ratios can vary with the ball, floor, and impact speed.
A small rise after a fall can tell us something about what happened at contact.

scenes.narration:
A falling ball returns, but not to where it began. Its bounce hides a square.

Ignore air resistance and imagine a rigid, still floor. Suppose the upward speed after impact is half the downward speed before it. That does not give half the original height.

Speed gained in falling grows with the square root of height. Going back upward reverses that relationship. Half the speed gives one quarter of the height.

This speed ratio is called the coefficient of restitution. In this simple model, the height ratio is its square. Energy also changes form during the collision, through deformation, warmth, and sound.

Try a speed ratio of three quarters instead. The returned height becomes nine sixteenths, a little over half. Real bounce ratios can vary with the ball, floor, and impact speed. A small rise after a fall can tell us something about what happened at contact.
